source_refs.note: Range of the projectile: a main subheading of 2.6 Projectile motion, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 34-37.

blocks.text: Maximum distance which a projectile covers in the horizontal direction is called the range of the projectile.

To determine the range R of the projectile, we multiply the horizontal component of the velocity of projection with total time taken by the body to hit the ground after leaving the point of projection. Thus

blocks.title: Do You Know ?
blocks.text: For an angle less than 45°, the height reached by the projectile and the range both will be less. When the angle of projectile is larger than 45°, the height attained will be more but the range is again less.

blocks.alt: Height against range for three projectiles fired with the same speed at 30, 45 and 60 degrees. The 60 degree path rises highest, the 45 degree path goes farthest, and the 30 and 60 degree paths land at the same point.
blocks.caption: Paths of projectiles fired at 30°, 45° and 60° (Do You Know; original drawing after the textbook's graph).

blocks.text_alt: or R = vi cos θ × 2vi sin θ / g
or R = (vi²/g) 2 sin θ cos θ

blocks.text: As 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ, thus the range of the projectile depends upon the velocity of projection and the angle of projection.
For maximum range R, the factor sin 2θ = 1, so
Air resistance will slow down projectile forward motion, reducing its velocity vi. The reduction in vi will result in a decrease in the range of projectile.

Furthermore, air resistance is not constant throughout the flight of the object. As the object slows down, the air resistance experienced by it also decreases. This means that the object retards more slowly and accelerates more slowly as it falls down. This results in a trajectory that is not perfectly parabolic but is skewed, with steeper descent than ascent.

blocks.title: For Your Information
blocks.text: In the presence of air friction the trajectory of a high speed projectile falls short of a parabolic path.

blocks.alt: Two paths from the same launch: the ideal path, a symmetric parabola, and the actual path with air friction, which rises less, comes down more steeply and lands short of the ideal one.
blocks.caption: Ideal path and actual path of a high-speed projectile (For Your Information; original drawing after the textbook's graph).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed graph draws the actual path with air friction almost symmetric, although the text says it is skewed, with a steeper descent than ascent. It is drawn skewed above.
Example: 2.5
A ball is thrown with a speed of 30 m s⁻¹ in a direction 30° above the horizon. Determine the height to which it rises, the time of flight and the horizontal range.
Solution: Initially
vix = vi cosθ = 30 m s⁻¹ × cos30° = 25.98 m s⁻¹
viy = vi sinθ = 30 m s⁻¹ × sin30° = 15 m s⁻¹
As the time of flight, is
t = 2vi sinθ / g
Height h = vi² sin²θ / 2g
Range R = (vi²/g) sin2θ = (vi²/g) sin60°
